questions.q: Which of these are valid ways to reference a column in PySpark?
options: A plain string, dot notation (df.col_name), and the col() function — all three work
Only col() works; strings and dot notation always fail
Only a plain string works; the other two are invalid syntax
None of these work without importing pandas first
questions.explain: All three produce the same result for a plain reference, but col() becomes necessary once you want to transform or rename the column.

questions.q: Why does .alias() require a col()-style reference instead of working on a plain string?
options: Because strings are immutable in Python
Because alias() only works on numeric columns
Because .alias() is a method that needs a Column object to call it on, and a plain string doesn't have that method
It doesn't require col() — plain strings support .alias() too
questions.explain: This is exactly why col() is introduced now — it's the gateway to renaming and transforming columns in later lessons.

questions.q: Is df.select("fare_amount") a transformation or an action?
options: A transformation — it builds a plan but doesn't execute anything until an action like .show() runs
Neither — select() doesn't exist in PySpark
An action — it immediately loads and prints the data
It depends on whether the DataFrame came from CSV or Parquet
questions.explain: This connects directly back to Lesson 34's lazy evaluation: select() builds the plan, .show() or .count() runs it.

questions.q: Why is selecting fewer columns from a Parquet-backed DataFrame especially efficient?
options: It isn't more efficient — Parquet always reads the entire file regardless
Because Parquet automatically deletes unselected columns from the file
Because select() converts the file to CSV first
Because Parquet's columnar storage means only the selected columns' bytes get read off disk, per Lesson 42
questions.explain: This ties directly back to Lesson 42's columnar storage explanation.
